title: Fair isle lap throw
subtitle: A 100 by 120 cm lap throw in all-over Fair Isle stranded colourwork, DK.
excerpt: A 100 by 120 cm lap throw worked flat in an all-over two-colour Fair Isle stranded pattern on 4 mm needles. The pattern uses a twenty-four-row, eight-stitch Shetland OXO repeat throughout. About 400 g of each of two DK colours. ADVANCED: managing consistent float tension across 220 stitches for 360 rows.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, 12th series (1896), §Fair Isle Stranded Colourwork, documents the OXO repeat as a classic Shetland pattern for blankets and shawls. The float-catching technique for flat fair isle is described in Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), §Fair Isle and Stranded Knitting.

knitting.gaugeText: 24 sts × 28 rows = 10 × 10 cm in Fair Isle stranded pattern on 4 mm needles, blocked. Stranded fabric is denser than stocking stitch at the same needle size.

glossaryTerms.definition: A classic Shetland stranded pattern where alternating O shapes (small diamond rings formed by four-stitch arcs in the contrast colour) and X shapes (cross-like patterns in the main colour) are arranged in a staggered grid over a 24-row, 8-stitch repeat. All floats within the repeat are five stitches or shorter, which is the self-contained float limit that avoids the need for catching.

content.text: A single-panel rectangle worked flat on 4 mm needles in an all-over two-colour
OXO Fair Isle repeat
, finishing at 100 cm wide by 120 cm long.

Single-panel construction; no seaming. All-over Fair Isle is ADVANCED because both colours are carried on every row across 240 stitches for the entire 336 rows, and consistent float tension is the sole difference between a flat, professional result and a puckered one. The OXO repeat was chosen because its maximum float is five stitches, which is within the self-catching limit; no deliberate float-catching is required. Stranded fabric is denser than single-colour stocking stitch, so the finished throw is warm and stable. Budget about 400 g per colour (about 880 m / 960 yards each). Buy in matched dye lots.
What you need

items.name: Main colour (MC)
items.qty: 400 g (about 880 m / 960 yards) of DK. A dark tone for the OXO outlines reads most clearly.

items.name: Contrast colour (CC)
items.qty: 400 g of DK in a light or warm contrasting tone

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 4 mm (UK 8 / US 6) circular needle, 120 cm or longer

items.name: Blocking mat and pins
items.qty: Required, stranded fabric needs blocking to open and even out

content.text: Gauge

24 stitches and 28 rows to 10 cm in two-colour Fair Isle on 4 mm needles, blocked. Stranded gauge is different from single-colour stocking stitch gauge; swatch the OXO repeat in both colours for at least 15 cm before casting on. Wash and block the swatch to measure true gauge.
At 24 stitches per 10 cm blocked, 100 cm requires 240 stitches (a multiple of 8). At 22 per 10 cm, use 216 stitches for the same finished width.

items.qty: knit (in the colour specified by the chart)

items.name: p
items.qty: purl (WS Fair Isle rows: purl each stitch in the chart colour)

content.text: Pattern
Cast-on
Using MC and the long-tail cast-on, cast on 240 stitches (a multiple of 8 for the OXO repeat). Long-tail tail: (4 × 240) / 10 + 15 = 96 + 15 = 111 cm. Measure 130 cm.
Body (24-row, 8-stitch OXO repeat)

RS rows: follow the OXO chart, carrying both MC and CC across the row. Spread the stitches across the right needle before knitting each one so floats lie at the natural stitch width and do not pull in.
WS rows: purl each stitch in its chart colour, carrying both yarns across the wrong side. Keep the floats consistent: they should lie at the same tension as the RS floats.

Repeat the 24-row cycle until the throw measures 120 cm, blocked. Work to 108 cm unblocked (the throw will gain about 10 to 12 cm in width and length with blocking). When you set this aside, note the row within the 24-row repeat.
Stitch count check-ins
At row 168 (about 60 cm): count across. You should have 240 stitches. Fair Isle never changes stitch count. At row 334 (about 119 cm): count again before casting off.
Common faults

Puckering across the full width: floats are too tight. The spread-stitches method is non-optional; every float must be laid at the natural width of the stitches it spans. Try going up one needle size (4.5 mm) if consistent puckering persists after spreading stitches.

OXO alignment failing after several rows: the 24-row count was lost after setting the work down. Use a row counter reset at row 1 of each new repeat, and verify the OXO diamond centres line up before continuing past row 12.
WS floats showing through to the RS on a pale CC: the WS floats were pulled too tight and pulled the MC stitches into gaps. On WS rows, spread the stitches as carefully as on RS rows.
Cast-off
Cast off with MC knitwise using needles one size larger. Cut CC after the last row.
Finishing

Weave in all ends on the wrong side, there are only two sets (cast-on and cast-off for each colour) if the yarns were carried throughout. Wet block the finished throw: soak, squeeze, pin to 100 × 120 cm, leave to dry fully (24 to 48 hours). The OXO pattern will clarify and even out considerably with blocking.
Care
Machine wash on a gentle 30-degree cycle for superwash DK. Lay flat to dry, reshaping to measurements. Re-block as needed if the pattern loses definition.
What to try next

From a two-colour Fair Isle throw, try a three-colour Shetland peerie-and-border throw. A wide border sits at top and bottom with a complex motif. A narrower peerie repeat fills the centre. Three colours combine in different ways across the rows.
